segments.text: When we came up with the theme for Democratic Newsroom and for the India Today Conclave South of a surging South, I think we've covered a myriad of topics over the last two days of economy, of startups, of human capital, and so much more that I think that's self-explanatory in itself on what makes the South stand out, which each of the states we've covered each have
their strength.

But I think what makes, to me at least, what makes the South stand out, and as someone who lives in Delhi now, and seeing all that's happened in the South, is because there's no way the North can compete with southern states who've invested very early on in human capital.
Now you've got northern states playing catch-up as a result.
Education.
healthcare, infrastructure, these are aspects that I think the southern states focused on very early on.
Today, the northern states seem to have woken up and said, okay, these are aspects we should be focusing on.
So I think it's a game of catch up.
And so in that sense, the south has surged, not surging, if you ask me.
Okay, fair enough.
I come from the western seaboard of this country and I could well argue that Maharashtra remains India's number one state when it comes to industrialization.
We had a huge advantage in terms of our infrastructure at the very outset.
And even within Maharashtra, you could argue that there are parts that are falling off and parts that are surging ahead.
And that's true of the entire country.
I think that's what I would like to say.
Rather than make this, you know, south versus north is an oversimplification.
There are parts of the north which are doing reasonably well.
There are parts which are falling behind.
Punjab was...
one of India's leading states in terms of the economy in the 1980s.
It slipped in the last 30 years.
The Bimaru states have always lagged behind.
Parts of Uttar Pradesh are slowly showing signs of an economic rise.
And therefore, it's an oversimplification to make this south versus north.
I mean, most of the southern states, as you've seen, are having huge revenue deficits.
Karnataka is struggling with all its guarantees.
Telangana is struggling.
Kerala is a state whose economy is not exactly right there at the top.
They've done very well on social indicators, but jobs is a big issue.
This is an aging society.
Why young Keralites moving out of Kerala?
So, Andhra Pradesh, desperately needed special status 10 years ago, didn't get it, is now slowly rebuilding.
So please don't make this south versus north as if south is a… you know… No, no.
First of all, Rajdeep, where is Maharashtra?
North of India, south of India.
Where is Maharashtra?
North of India, south of India.
We are the western seaboard.
Please give us some space.
Maharashtra is definitely… Sorry?
Goa, Goa.

Goa we treat as part of our western seaboard now I know that there are people who want Goa to be part and there are those who argued India today South should also reflect Goa I mean when you have the Ranji Trophy tournament and zones were divided Goa interestingly used to be in the South Zone for the longest time my limited point is India has
Islands of prosperity that have got, as you rightly said, understood the importance of human development early on.
But there are also large areas and large parts of India which have lagged behind across this country.
Look at the eastern part of the country.
which has also lagged behind significantly.
So I'm going to draw what one economist said is a Kanpur line.
And you've got to look at India this side of the Kanpur line and that side of the Kanpur line and there's a huge difference.
You spoke about revenue deficits of all the southern parts of India, Karnataka, Kerala, Andhra.
That's because in the last 25-30 years, the central government, irrespective of the party, is not paying our taxes back.
The devolution is that on our money, someone else is getting developed.
And that's the reason we are having revenue deficits.
We are also giving back to the people the direct benefit transfers, but still we are not getting back the money that we pay as taxes.
Look at… Nagat, that's a very simple… That's the only North Indian now, Preeti, you're really the only North Indian in this debate because the truth of the matter… I love the South.
No pressure, Preeti, no pressure.
No, no, Raj asked me about Goa.
Truth is, when I'm in the South, I feel very comfortable.
There is something about being South, Southern comfort.
I am…
a western, west Indian who is very comfortable in the south.
That's why we call it the southwest monsoon.
We see the southwest monsoon come from Kerala towards Maharashtra and I feel that life is, you know, you almost feel a sense of new energy.
So the one north Indian from Haryana is here with us.
So naturally she wants to defend, she wants to defend the double engine model.
No, nobody wants to defend any double engine model.
Just one second, Priti.
Before Akshita asked, is Maharashtra part of
southern part of India or is it northern part of India?
The only bifurcation is not the Vindhyas.
Do you understand Hindi or not?
That's the big barrier, I think.
Now it's consideration.
If you don't understand Hindi, I think you are a part of southern part of India.
You know, I think that's very simplistic.
Okay, now yes, Rajdeep has nicely bailed out of the north versus south divide saying, I'm from Maharashtra.
You guys figure it out.
But, okay, so I am from the north and I think it's oversimplification, A, to suggest with what Naga is saying that certain southern states bail out
the northern states, the poorer states, which some of the northern states are poorer.
Why I think it's over simplistic and why I think one needs to look at each state in itself.
Okay, I'll give you an example.
What I love about the South and how it invests in its human capital.
I took a flight right now and I was coming in from the Kochi airport and my driver tells me that you're not allowed to honk.
It's a traffic violation in Kerala if you actually honk.
And there are AI cameras everywhere that actually pick up.
And in 15 minutes, if I honk, I'm going to get a chalan.
And I was astounded, because this to me was a developed country, kind of a norm, right?
And I'm thinking back home, you get into
If I take a flight from Delhi to Banaras, the first thing the driver does is sit on his horn.
So there are very different facets to what is the south, what is the north in terms of human capital development.
But I'll give you an example.
For example, yes, you might add more to the financial kitty naga.
I'll give you an example of my states.
Haryana and adds more of medals in Olympics to our country.
So does that make your contribution more and mine lesser or mine more or your lesser?
No.
I just add something very different to it, which adds to your country.

Punjab, in terms of agriculture, has been adding parts of Uttar Pradesh, has been adding to agriculture for a very long time, which possibly parts of the south doesn't add, doesn't make one better than the other.
this thing in the sense that we can both learn from each other.
That's my point, right?
In terms of human development, certainly the north can learn a lot from the south.
You can see it quite clearly, literacy levels.
Take a look at per capita income levels also when you look at economic distinctions.
I think we are an average in the south about three lakhs and say Uttar Pradesh is about one lakh per capita.
So you can see the distinctions there.
Of course, let's not forget that the northern states have far more political weight.
Southern states, even if they give the Congress a majority or whatever other party, they cannot form a party in the center.
But that's something that they leverage.
The north does leverage it.
The south tries to fight back.
But of course, to correct Nagar,

The fact was that yes, for a long time, the South was getting the wrong end of the stick when it came to finances, but I think the 16th Finance Commission corrected that anomaly by introducing the 10% GDP criteria.
So in some senses, the South got a little more this time of the entire thing.
But if you take a look at some of the larger issues that we had to look at, when I was saying the comparisons,
The North, because it's starting off fresh, you see a lot of investment getting into Uttar Pradesh, into Bihar, into other places that's there, where we need to learn.
We are very good at capturing investment.
We dominate, I think, 66% of electronics, 66% of IT, or whatever that is.
But North is beginning to wake up.
Uttar Pradesh is beginning to wake up considerably.
So is other states.
And again, North, you have to be very careful, because
As in the south, we shouldn't treat ourselves as homogeneous units.
I am from Karnataka, Akshita could be from Kerala, you could be from Andhra, and these are all separate states that do their... There can't be a Varna system in states.
There cannot be a caste system in states that certain castes are more hierarchical.

say not for instance Haryana had a very high per capita income so did Punjab for a while and Uttar Pradesh and Bihar are different states so you can't really make the distinction so easily but the fact is I think both of us need to learn from each other there are points that are very good across like you said sports out there and there are negatives that the you know the north can learn and correct itself when looking at the south
Chibi, you want to come in?
I think one of the questions is when we speak of southern states that Kerala is lagging behind.
Do you want to answer that?
Yeah, that's also because we invest a lot in education and the skilled labor is too high.
Much before any other state, we invest a lot in education that we have far too many skilled labor that people keep teasing us that we go abroad in search of jobs.
That's also because we are qualified in that way.
You get those jobs.

Yes, get those jobs so that way and also Naga was mentioning about us bailing out in terms of contribution to the economy but also we have also implemented the population policy and all the other policies properly since many decades and I think now we're getting punished for it also in you know with measures like delimitation where we don't have any say so that's also concerning for us as people coming from south where we don't get to have a major say in who's going to govern us.
No, I think she's making a very important point.
I think you're sensing this among a number of the southern politicians.
Why are you – I won't use the word – they use the word penalize, but how will you incentivize us?

You see, if we are contributing more to the national exchequer in terms of collection of taxes, in terms of the revenue receipts in our states, how are you going to ensure that we have a greater say in what happens in Delhi?
That is going to become a major conflict point because the fact is at the moment the BJP and its allies are largely dominated in and around the northern belt of the country.
They are northern and western India and now east is where the BJP gets most of its MPs from.
So you don't have enough MPs also, ministers now also coming in from the south in comparison to what it was 20, 25 years ago when there was a UPA government, United Front government.
You need that balance.
For a federal balance, I think, it is important to incentivize the states of the south for their high growth numbers, for their better social indicators.
How, Rajdeep?
How do you incentivize?
Because everyone's been coming up with different permutations, combinations, but ultimately the theme you're right is that there should be fairness.
I mean the finance commission, 16th finance commission has taken steps in that direction.
Maybe much more needs to be done.
But I think you need to also bridge the social and cultural divide.
You know, this imposition of Hindi for example.
Many believe that there is still this feeling of Hindi, Hindu, Hindustan.
That needs to go.
That's yesterday's story.
That cannot be the story of today's India.
Today's India has to be able to accommodate people across the linguistic divide.
Just because Hindi cannot be imposed on the South, I think that debate has to go away.
Interestingly, people from the North are migrating to the South.
You go to Uttakamand or Ooty,
as it's Uttakamand of course was earlier, Ooty, all the labor are all from Bihar.
So that migration is taking place from north to south.
People are bridging the divide.
Politicians also need to do more.
Politicians do not need to talk the language only of the Hindi heartland.
They must talk.
For example, we are in Kerala, right?
There may be people in this audience who like their beef curry.
They're perfectly entitled to have their beef curry.
I don't want Delhi to be deciding what my food habits are.
Don't eat this, don't do that.
All of that has to stop.
They cannot be detected from Delhi.
Delhi cannot detect this country.
India is a country that lives in the States.
I totally agree with you, but then also there cannot be a sense of superiority complex that stems from the southern states over the northern states.
That cannot happen.
But the imposition needs to go, I 100% agree with you and I think it also somewhere down the line stems from the fact that the power centre of the country has been the north.
And whether we like it or not like it and that is where the insecurity of the south stems from.
So yes, imposition no, but there cannot be a superiority complex like I said just because
There cannot be a Varna system in states.
You cannot have a Brahmanical order in how you judge states in this country.
I'll tell you one, I'll give you an example.
I live in Delhi.
So many times do I know, I admit that the standard of living this side of the Vindhyas is so much better than the north.
So many times I would say that I'd like to go and live in the south, right?
But where do I see true resilience and of the human spirit?
It is in states in the north which actually show you where they rise from, and that's what makes our country.
But Preeti, I would, I mean just to add what Rajdeep had said, he talked of various divides, but I would look at it as also a GDP divide.
And if you take a look at the GDP of, say, Tamil Nadu, it's something like 17 trillion, right?
And if you take a look at, which is about a third of the size of Uttar Pradesh.
In Uttar Pradesh, GDP right now is around 18 trillion.
So you can see that there is things that they need to look at as to why the South grew the way it did, despite the fact that only 18% of India's population contributes 30% of its GDP.
So there is a GDP divide which each of those states need to study how we figured it out and did the kind of things we did.
There is a certain discipline in the south that you don't find, you know, not very obvious in the north.
There's a commitment to work, they get up early enough, they go and do their things and there's no...

Can I just highlight here that the superiority complex that Preeti was referring to, among the southern states, it's very easy for each state to hate each other and have that same fight that, okay, no, this state has a certain language, we have a different language, we have a different culture because you'll find that in each southern state.
But you will see instead a healthy competition.
Why is that?
Because nobody looks down on the other.
When someone from a Delhi comes down to Chennai and speaks to them in Hindi and says, Aise hi baat karunga mein.
Why don't you know Hindi?
That is a problem.
No, just two.
No, just two.
That creates a mindset among the people.
That creates a mindset.
We began this debate with Naga Arjuna saying, of course south is better.
So there is a sense of superiority.
The big topic is South better than the North.
Do you understand?
That's the topic.
So when it comes to… And yes, a lot of markers, and I agree with you, Naga, a lot of markers when it comes down to the human capital in this state, we will admit South is better.
That doesn't make it superior.
You spoke about Varna system.
Nobody said superior.
Nobody used the word superior.
I'm agreeing with you, Varna.
And my simple point is… It started like that.
It started like that.
You said South is better.
Listen to me, we have to… it's not Varna system.
We are in fact feeling alienated.
In the next thirty years, I don't even know if a southern individual or politician can become the prime minister of this country.
That's alienation.
That's alienation.
That's not superiority complex.
I'm saying… Are you telling me… Are you telling me… Don't look down upon… Listen to me.
Listen to me.
Listen to me.
Listen to me.
Listen to me.
Listen to me.
Listen to me.
Listen to me.
Listen to me.
Listen to me.
Listen to me.
In fact, it's the other way around.
People are looking down upon us.
We are not looking down upon UP or Bihar or Rajasthan.
They are looking down upon us.
Like how Akshita said that you have to speak this language, you have to do this.
That's imposition.
Imposition needs to stop.
That's it.
Imposition needs to stop.
We go to North Indian states, we never ask them to speak in our language.
Agree?
I go there and speak in Hindi.
Yeah, like you try and speak in their language.
That's how you do it, right?
And when people come here and tell us like, you know, Hindi mein baat karo,
And that's not… Find a common language.
Let's talk in English.
I don't know.
I don't know, Malayalam.
That's the argument that we have been putting forward.
Let's talk in English.
Shruti, while you agree, most of the others don't.
In the near future, after delimitation, do you think a southern politician can ever be a prime minister of India if there's 800 seats in the parliament?
See, after Deva Gowda became prime minister, one Maharashtra politician told me he realized anyone can become prime minister tomorrow.
Because Deva Gowda was at the right place at the right time.
He was a powerful leader, of course, of Karnataka.
Let's not forget Narsimha Rao.
Yeah, Narsimha Rao became prime minister also.
So I'm not going to write of who becomes a prime minister tomorrow.
If you told me 25 years ago that Narendra Modi would be the leader number one of the BJP, you'd probably not have put him in the front row.
But he is now a very successful prime minister of the Bharatiya Chantapati.
But I think your larger point is well taken, that if delimitation goes through in the present form, there is a huge imbalance between North and South.
And I think that should be a matter of concern.
I really think that the genius of this country is its pluralism.
You know, I see it in the food, in the diversity of the sheer food.
Look at the way fish is cooked here in Kerala.
Look at the way fish is cooked in Goa.
Look at the way it's cooked in Bengal.
In every part of the country, the fish is cooked differently.
You come to Amritsar and you'll get, you know, in Makhan, a very different kind of fish.
India's genius and the greatness of this country is the diversity.
We can have this endless debate, South versus North.
The truth of it is reflected in Tagore's Janaka Namana.
He reflects the genius of a country coming together.
My worry is politicians are the ones who divide us.
They are the ones.
It was a politician who came to Kerala and said, what?
It will become a Somalia?
What did he say?
I won't name him.
No, no Rajdeep.
Kerala is Somalia.
Imagine which world is this politician living in that he could come to the wonderful land of Kerala and try to liken it to Somalia.
This is the… it is the politicians who are dividing us, not the people.
Away from the superiority complex.
Coming back to it, I feel there cannot be no snobbery attached even where the North is concerned or the South.
There has to be diversity and one has to respect diversity of each of our states.
Who's surging?
Sorry?
Who is surging then?
Is the North surging ahead?
Is the South surging ahead?
We can't be caught in the binary of who's surging ahead.
The fact is as long as India is surging ahead, and each – like I said, I'll come again.
I can turn around and say I don't need a Kerala because Haryana is getting in all the medals.
So I can fight as a country on my own.
The medals don't fuel the economy also.
So Haryana is surging ahead.
I can't – I don't want to – you can't be caught into the binary of who's surging ahead.
I think maybe let's define surge here, okay?
in the sense of growth.
Again, I'll come back to it.
What are your benchmarks on growth?
Because if you're only going to look at it in terms of just standard of living or you're going to look at it in terms of fiscally on how much you're adding to the fiscal kitty,
No, you can't look at it on that, right?
Because there are different parameters of growth.
And like I said, sports is a parameter.
Agriculture is a parameter.
Human resilience, I feel, of the human spirit is a parameter.
You see it in states away from the south as well.
I respect the south.
There is diversity there.
I think there has to be pluralism and no imposition.
That I strongly oppose.
Zero imposition.
I tried to get Preeti to admit South is searching, it didn't work.
There is a truth, and the truth is that yes, the South has taken the lead on various sectors across, whether income, health, education.
You look across, there's certainly a lead, but it's also a trap.

because the South shouldn't get complacent because if you see the way both Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and others have rapidly changed their demographics as well as their investment factors and others, it shouldn't mean that we lead today and we yield tomorrow to the North.
I think the South has to watch out for that complacency.
I don't think it's complacency.
I think we have seen how industries are being lured into the northern states or at least directed towards those states.
The companies themselves have spoken.
The politicians have spoken.
If it's a playing field, I think the southern states will do much, much more better.
It's not superiority complex.
It's rather inferior to that we are being alienated in the mainstream
politics, mainstream finances, that we need to get our due share, be it language, culture, economy or any dividend in politics also.
And that's where I'm saying, South will surge, we need our share right away.
Final word, Rajdeep.
My final word is that I am just happy to be an Indian.
I was born in Ahmedabad, where I never thought that Gujarat would become the political center of gravity of the country at the time.
I grew up in Mumbai and it still remains my favorite city.
My dad came from a small town in Goa.
So I'm a West Indian in that sense, but I wouldn't have got any professional achievements but for the fact that I spent three decades in Delhi.
So Delhi has been very good to me.
and I was able to discover the Hindi heartland.
And in the last few decades, I've also discovered the wondrous nature of the South.
Only last week or 10 days ago, I found out that the Kerala's Chief Minister's favourite author is Oran Pamuk.
Now, I mean, I never thought that I would see a Chief Minister of a state and he was serious about it because I went on a flight back with him and he was reading the book.
So here is a chief minister who is a bibliophile.
It just makes me feel hopeful about India.
You know in India we look at the glass half empty.
South versus north.
South is surging, north is falling.
It's healthy.
Rajdeep, it's good to have that competition.
You want others to surge ahead.
You want others to feel relieved.
Competition ma'am should be on a level playing field.
No, there should be no double engine, triple engine format.
Every state must get equal rights.
Every state is part of this country.
You cannot differentiate between states.
One is opposition, one is rule.
That is my problem.
This discriminatory federalism must not be there.
It must be genuine cooperative federalism.
celebrate the fact that we are this unique diverse society in the world.
Have the best breakfast that you can have in Kerala.
No one can beat the Kerala breakfast.
Have the best fish that you can have here.
But also go back to Delhi and have your butter chicken and whatever else.
Just realize the preciousness of our diversity.
I don't think we realize what a precious treasure this country is.
So I, on that note, I'm going to withdraw from this South versus North debate.
because I believe at the end of the day, we are all Indians.
Jai ho!
We can have Indian 3, next Indian 3 movie with Rajdeep starring in it.
Hey, yesterday 4 by 400 meter relay, all those women.
Amazing, I agree.
I mean, they were all from different parts of India, including I think one of them from Kerala itself.
Tamil Nadu.
She's a long jump.
The girl from Tamil Nadu ran the last lap.
Kerala was a long jump.
Anchor.
But you know, you look at our Indian team, why does India, my final word, why does India do so well in cricket?
Because now India has discovered the true power of the democratization of the sport.
So you can find a genius, you know, you can find a talent like Sanju Samson here.
You can find a Rishabh Pant in some other part of the country and you will find talents from each and every corner.
That's what we should be looking for.
Looking at reflecting the genius of a land like no other.
And I maintain our Netas are part of the problem.
Angre is chalega with their divide and rule.
They still carry it on even today.
Okay, great message, unifying message there for Rajni, but we'll keep this truly democratic.
Show of hands.
I'll come back to the same question.
Is South surging ahead of the others?
A show of hands if you say yes.
Yeah, I'm asking them show of hands.
I mean, we're in Kerala, so I'm not going to read into that, but thank you so much.
Thank you everyone for indulging us in this democratic news.
